title.en: Why живой changes with its noun

summary.en: Treat the adjective ending as a clue to the noun beside it.

body.en:
From season 1, episode 3.

The live goose in episode 3 gives a clear adjective–noun pair: **живой гусь**. **гусь** is grammatically masculine, so the adjective uses a masculine nominative singular form here.

Russian adjectives normally agree with the noun they describe in gender, number and case. The adjective can therefore change even though its basic meaning stays the same. Start by noticing the noun; then interpret the adjective's ending in relation to it.

Common nominative singular adjective patterns include masculine **-ый/-ий/-ой**, feminine **-ая/-яя** and neuter **-ое/-ее**. These are recognition patterns, not instructions for mechanically changing any word; spelling and stress also matter.

Do not use the adjective ending to guess the real-world sex of every object. Agreement follows grammatical gender. On a replay, locate the describing word, locate its noun, and ask whether the pair refers to one thing or several.
